With respect to clause C of section I, which does away with the use of voters' lists within sixty days previous to the election, I mean to allow the law to stand as it is, so that clause C will he struck out.
Hear, hear.

Has the Solicitor General any provision in this Bill with reference to lists which may have been quashed after they have been sent to the office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery ? On or about the 24th of December in each year, in New Brunswick, the list is filed with the proper officer, and is forwarded by him to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. Suppose that list is quashed in the meantime, is there any provision whereby a new list shall be ordered to be forwarded from the custodian to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery ?

Under the law as it now stands, the custodian forwards the list to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery after it has become law within the limits of the province. It is impossible that a list subsequently quashed should go to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, because it only goes to him after the delay for the appeal has expired, or after the appeal has been disposed of.

The circumstances are somewhat different in the county of King's, N.B. The lists were completed in that county and filed by the secretary-treasurer with the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. It was completed on the 24th December last. After that date, and at the February term of the Supreme Court of New Brunswick, that list was brought before the court in connection with the parish of Rothesay and quashed. The right hon. the premier, in answer to a question I put on the Order paper, stated that the government had no notice of the quashing of that list. As a matter of fact in this list that was quashed there were over 400 voters' names added. According to the answer of the premier, that list is now on file with the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. The seat I have the honour to hold in this House is protested. There is a petition filed against me, and suppose that petition were successful, and I were unseated, and that a new election would take place during this summer,
and before the filing of the new list, this bogus list is the list which would be used in the election.
No.

Why not? The Clerk of the Crown in Chancery sends down the list to the returning officer, but if there is no official notification of the quashing of that list, and if the officer in charge of the list in King's has done his duty, there is nothing in the law to require him to send the amended list.
Yes.

I do not see anything in the law to that effect, and I propose you should amend it to cover that point. Here are the facts. This list was quashed in February. A new list has been made up, but it is not the list which is on file here. You adopt the provincial list, but send it out as a Dominion list; and the list is the one which was on file on the 24th of December last.

would call the hon. gentleman's attention to section 10 of the Franchise Act, which provides :
Within ten days after the final revision of every list of voters for the purposes of provincial elections, it shall be the duty of the custodian thereof to transmit to the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, by registered mail, a copy of such list, certified under the hand of such custodian.
If he has sent a list which was subsequently set aside by the courts, and a new list has been declared by the courts to be applicable to the particular district, the new list is the list in force, and that is the list Which he must send to the Clerk of the Grown in Chancery. The previous list, which was set aside, is absolutely waste paper.

Mr. FOWLER, Still, the list which was filed on the 24th of December is the list which exists at present.

It is prepared under a special enactment. The voters' list was

stuffed by the wrongful act of the reviser. It was a most .scoundrelly piece of business, and no honest or decent Liberal would attempt for a moment to defend it. By collusion with the reviser, after the list went from the revising board and before it reach ed the secretary-treasurer, it was taken to an office in St. John and altered. Some 400 names of parties who had no right to vote in the county of King's were added to it. The sworn certificate, which was on a separate piece of paper, had been taken off, the new list was made up, the certificate attached to it again, and then it was sent forward to the secretary-treasurer. That list came before the Supreme Court, and the court at once, on a presentation of the facts by affidavit, set it aside.
Therefore that list ceased to exist.

By a special Act of the local legislature it was ordered that the revisers of the parish prepare a new list, but the list as prepared is not on file in the office of the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery.
That is the list in force.

It would be the list in force for a provincial election, but it is not the list for a Dominion election, unless the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery lias official notification of it. I inquired about that, and I was told by the premier that the only list here is the one filed on tlie 24th of December.

As I understand the case, the electoral list is properly revised by the board of revisers. It falls into tlie bands of some evil persons who tamper with it. Application is made to the court, and the court orders that list to he set aside. Therefore that list has ceased to exist so far as the province is concerned. Then application is made to the legislature, and the legislature passes a Bill which has application to the list for that particular polling division. Therefore, so far as the province is concerned, the list authorized by the legislature is the one in force. In that event, the returning officer, when he receives the writ, pays no attention to the copy of the list which was sent to him by the Clerk of tlie Crown in Chancery, but under section 22 of the Elections Act he applies to the legal custodian of the last list in force, being the list made under the provision of the Act of the legislature, and that is the list he must use for the purposes of an election.

The returning officer is an official of the 'Federal authorities ; therefore he looks to the Federal authorities for his list. He is not supposed to go around to find out what changes have been made
in the list, or if any changes have been made in it. He is supposed to take the list which he receives from the authority under which he is acting. Therefore he takes the list which he receives from the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery. I think this difficulty could be very easily provided for, and

2	of section 10 of this Act. (61 Vic., chapter 4.)

I have an amendment here, which has to do with this section, providing for the form of oath which a voter will be required to take whose name is omitted on account of provincial disqualification. It is an amendment of the form I in the Dominion Election Act.

much more difficult for the ordinary voter to understand. Perhaps if I would read the amendment which I introduced, the hon. gentleman would seize my meaning better. The amendment I propose reads thus :

Provided, however, that it shall be sufficient if any one or more of the four paragraphs A, B, C and D in the .said form are included in such oath, the remaining paragraphs being eliminated therefrom.
My intention was that when a voter came in whose name was not on the list, and who desired to take this oath, he would be asked which of the four reasons he would assign for his name being left off the list. He has to select one or more of the four, mentioned in the Franchise Act. The best way to dispose of the matter would be for my hon. friend to call on Mr. Fraser of the Justice Department and talk it over with him, and then together draft an amendment which would meet the case. I am not wedded to the form I have suggested at all.

Any person belonging to or engaged in any profession, calling, occupation, and so on.

meat will be at pains to ascertain whether or not the enactments of this section should be called into force.

The Secretary of State.

one year before tbe day fixed for tbe nomination,' and so on. Why have it a year before the writ in one case, and a year before the nomination in the other case ?

The MINISTER OF MARINE AND r ISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) moved that certain amendments made by the Senate to Bill (No. 92) to further amend the Act respecting the safety of ships, be concurred in. He said :	I saw the gentlemen in the Senate who are connected with the shipping interests and who proposed that the law should he in the direction of affording greater protection to shippers. The law lias stood for many years, and there is a strong objection against deckloads on ships going to Great Britain or to the northern part of Europe, and from time to time amendments were made taking out of that prohibition certain parts of the world such as Newfoundland, the United States of America, St. Pierre or Miquelon, the West Indies and South America. It was brought to my attention that some of our ships will be going to | Australia and carrying deck-loads, and some of our ships will be going to tlie Cape of Good Hope and carrying deck-loads, and others will he competing with the United States in the wood trade in the Mediterranean sea. It was suggested by a large number of senators, and in the suggestion

I concur, that it would be better to confine the limitation entirely to the 'British Isles and to the northern ports of Europe, so that there will be no prohibition upon deck-loads to any other part of the world except the British Isles and to the northern parts of Europe, and in that case our ships will be able to compete on an equal footing and without discrimination with the ships sailing from Boston, Portland and elsewhere. It does seem to me, when you come to think it over, unfair to prohibit a ship from carrying six feet of deck-load to the Cape of Good Hope or to a point in the Mediterranean sea, neither of which voyages are dangerous, while you permit them to go to any part of South America, or to the West Indies, or to Newfoundland. The amendment, therefore, they suggested would be simply to confine the prohibition to ships .sailing to a port in the British Isles or to a port in Europe north of Cape Finisterre, not being a port in the Mediterranean. The meaning of that would be that the limitation upon the deck-load carried would he confined entirely to ships sailing to the British Isles and to ports in Europe north of Cape Finisterre, but not including any part of the Mediterranean sea.
The result would be this, that a ship going to Jamaica
Would not be under the operation of that Act.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Whereas one going to Cuba

Would not be under tbe operation. If tlie amendment is accepted, there would be no prohibition upon deckloads carried by our ships to any part of the world except they are going to the British Isles or to a northern port in Europe.

When one wants to know what is prohibited and what is not, ho finds that in subsections (a) and (b), the articles that are prohibited in any part of the ship; he finds in subsection (c) the prohibited articles in uninclosed spaces, and he finds in subsection (d) the prohibited articles in inclosed spaces.

This is the crucial period. Now is the time when the men are going out to work in the lobster factories and in the fisheries along the coast, and now is the time when they" should have the accommodation that they are asking for. I trust the hon. gentleman will see that this accommodation is afforded without first waiting to consult the superintendent of the Prince Edward Island Railway, because he has his chief engineer here, i trust that he will promise now. for the purpose of expediting the public business, because I do not want to take up any time in connection with this matter, that he will put this train on the road immediately. If the hon. gentleman will put a second train on this part of the railway he will give the commercial interests of Summerside and Charlottetown the accommodation that they require.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS'AND CANALS. I will give it as favourable consideration as possible. The hon. gentleman must know that in all railway operations there are certain seasons in which it is found most expedient and most in the interests of the railway service, as well as of the public, to change our trains. These periods have been found, after many years' experience, to be the best suited to the purpose, and, having been recognized by our experience and practice heretofore, I would not undertake to say off-hand that it would be expedient to change that usage. I do say, however, that I will give it as favour- . able consideration as possible, and I think the hon. gentleman must be satisfied with that.

Well, of course, I must be satisfied with whatever the hon. minister says. As I said before, we are now on the threshold of the twentieth century. The people of the western part of Prince Edward Island were the first to move in connection with the building of the railway, and they are the most neglected of any people on Prince Edward Island. They are neglected in this way.
You were speaking of the Charlottetown business people a moment ago.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Yes, Sir, these business men in Charlottetown and the eastern part of the province have interests west of Summerside. On the success of their business depends largely the interests of the people of West Prince. If these people who have enterprise are going to develop the resources of that part of the country they should have some assistance from the government. Take the men from Charlottetown. The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries, if he will listen to me for a moment, will know them. Take Mr. Wallace Longworth, who has factories at West Point. He does an extensive business. He is twelve miles from the railway. He must have his mails, and he waits each evening for these mails to arrive. They go to Charlottetown first, a distance of fifty miles, are there assorted and sent back next morning, and he will receive them on the following evening. At this time of advancement this is not in keeping with what we should have in Canada. We had great difficulty last winter in connection with this part of the railway. I brought the matter up in this honourable House some time ago. pointing out that for twelve days, at Tignish. in the western part of the country, we had no train. I was told that it was on account of the severe snowstorms that prevailed. AVhat did I see in the newspapers ? I saw that which convinced me that this was not a sufficient excuse for the stopping of these trains, because there were plenty of men I in that section of the country who would

have keen glad of a day's work shovelling snow, and of an opportunity of earning a dollar from this government. In order that it might be shown that we are living in a cold country, the superintendent of this railway was there with an artist and his kodac taking snapshots of the snow banks along the railway.

Does the hon. gentleman deny that there were the largest snow banks there ever known in the western end of the island. What is the use of denying the facts ?
* Mr. HACKETT. There were large snow banks, but there were large snow banks there in previous years also. For twenty years that railway has been operated and never before were the people of the western part of the province deprived of their mails and freight for twelve days.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Were there not hundreds of men employed there shovelling snow all the time. The hon. gentleman does not, I am sure, want to misrepresent the facts to the House, and I appeal to his sense of fair-play. Does he not believe that the superintendent used every possible exertion to get the road clear of snow, and that hundreds of men were employed ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
My information is that the superintendent said there was no money at his disposal to employ men. I do not know whether that is correct or not. I do know that while the superintendent was short of funds at that time, that previous to the election he had plenty of money to weed out the thistles and weeds growing along that line. They had hundreds of men employed along the line from Tignisli to Souris. These weeds and thistles along the line never gave any trouble before, but just before the election men were employed pulling them out so as to influence them in favour of the government candidates. When I was canvassing in October last, I came to a railway station, and I saw some thirty or forty mein sitting around having their lunch.
I went to a friend of mine and asked what the men were doing, and he told me they were weeding out the thistles and that I should see if some of my men were there and And out how they were going to vote.
I went among these men and I knew every one of them. I found that they were chiefly Liberals. There were the weak-kneed Liberals who were asked for some work previous to the election, and who if they did not receive that work might have voted against the government.
You would have them do such a calamitous thing as that ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We have more calamitous things than that, and you will find some

calamities occur very shortly. I found that some of these men were Conservatives, and I asked them: How are you going to vote ? They told me that neighbour So and So came to them and said that they could get work on the railway. I said : Did they ask you for your vote, and they replied : Yes, we were told that if we would vote for the government candidate we would get work on the government railway. Two of these men were Conservatives to my knowledge, and they possibly voted against me. They were poor men who were looking for a day's work and they accepted the offer of the agents of the government. The money that should have been expended io clearing the snow from the track was expended for the purpose of securing support for the government candidates not only in West Prince but in East Prince as well. If the minister wants to do justice to the people of West Prince and in order that we) may expedite business, I hope he may see his way clear to order two trains a day.
I wish to ask the minister a question with reference to a matter that has passed. What is the name of the owner of the land near St. John which is proposed to be taken for railway purposes ?
I have not the faintest idea.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I had an inquiry as to who was the owner. You do not know ?

I do not.
To straighten -line near Blue Shank, $10,000. Hon. Mr. HAGGART. I see you expended $3,000 last year and you ask $10,000 this year. How much will it shorten the line ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Taking away the three very sharp curves it will shorten the line about 1,000 feet. There are six curves altogether in that distance. Any one who knows just what six curves in a thousand feet mean will be ready to assent to the proposition that the line should be straightened at that point.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How long is the new line ?
It is a thousand feet we are straightening.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We gain a thousand feet, but what is the total length ?
Less than 10,000 feet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is this not the place where an accident occurred last year and where the engine driver was killed ?
I think not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think it is. I was over the lime a day or two afterwards, and I saw the remains of the wreck and it was there where the engine driver was killed. Was the section foreman who had been employed by the late! government previous to 1896, the section foreman who had charge of the track when this accident occurred ?
I would like the hon. gentleman to ask me something easy.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister always likes to have something easy. My information is that there had been a change of section foreman, that the new man in charge of the section was incapable and that the accident occurred and the man killed in consequence of the track being run down and neglected. That may not be an easy question for the minister to answer, but I can tell him that since 1874 that curve was on the Prince Edward Island Railway and no accident occurred previous to that.
There is always a first time you know.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There is always a first time, and it makes an excuse for a man who does not wish to do what is right and keep at work the experienced men who understand the track. In West Prince there was not a good man on that section of the line but was ruthlessly dismissed by this government-what for ? Not in the interest of the railway nor in the public interest, but for the purpose of giving employment to their own heelers and camp followers, who followed them around and worked for them during the elections. They care nothing for the life and limbs and property of the public. I say it should be publicly condemned that this railway should be placed under the control of party heelers and camp followers, and the lives and limbs of our people endangered. And yet the minister says, Ask me something easy.

I think I may fairly say that I know something of the appointments which have been made on the Prince Edward Island Railway since 1896, and I say unhesitatingly that there never has been a section foreman changed for political reasons since 1896 ; I do not know what took place before that. The section foremen have all been retained ; and if any have been dismissed, it must have been for purely railway reasons, and not for political reasons. The hon. gentleman knows that some of the railway trackmasters have been there since 1874, as well as all the leading officials. The great complaint in Prince Edward Island is, that Tories have been allowed to remain in almost all the offices.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I know what I am talking about.
Give me the name of one section foreman who has been dismissed for political reasons.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I will give the names of two who were dismissed for no other reason than that they were Conservatives : Peter L. Cliesson, between Tignish and Al-berton, and Robert McLean, between Al-berton and Bloomfield. Put their names down. I could go along the whole line between Summerside and Tignish, and give, not only the names of foremen, but experienced workmen, sectionmen and labourers, who were dismissed, and others put in their place. It is a shameful and disgraceful thing ; and yet, the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals says, Ask me something easy.
The hon. minister has not given me the information I asked for : what is the distance between the two points ?
I told the hon. gentleman between 8,000 and 10,000 feet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And you have shortened it a few feet, and reduced some of the gradients at this particular point V

The grade is maintained, but we are reducing the curvature.
To provide and lay steel rails and fastenings,
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This item is an error, which occurred in transferring the figures to the printed estimates. It ought to be $36,000. I shall have to take the other $30,000 in the supplementary estimates. We are proposing to put on the Island railway the 56-pound rails which we are taking up from the Drummond County Railway, and which are very superior rails, and in excellent condition. We are charging these rails at the same price at which we credit the Intercolonial account.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is, $15 a ton, is it not ?

No, these rails are put in at $26. There will be 2,750 tons of these, which, at $26 a ton, amount to $76,200 ; and we credit the old rails which we take up at $12 a ton ; so that the difference will be $14 a ton.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
If I remember rightly, the rails on the Prince Edward Island Railway must have cost us about $90 a ton, and they were the finest rails ever laid on a track. I found out to-day for the first time that the steel rails taken from the Drummond County Railway were credited to the stores account of the Intercolonial,



at $26 a ton. I was making my calculations on all tlie rails supplied or renewed on tlie Intercolonial, at $15 a ton, and I would like tlie minister to give the exact quantities of both, and tlie amounts credited in the stores account.
Prince Edward Island Railway-To provide machinery, $5,000.
Wliat machinery Is wanted ?

We are doing our repairs in the workshops at Charlottetown, and we require to put in some additional machinery, in the shape of planers, mortisers, bolt cutters, boring machines, rail cutters, and a compressed air plant, &c.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When I was looking at the shops there I thought there was machinery enough. All your serious repairs should be made at Moncton. It is a waste of money to have extensive repair shops for a little railway like that.

The bon. gentleman is not correct in that statement. I selected two or three competent people a year or so ago to visit the shops at Charlottetown and make their report. They reported to me favourably on the shops-that they were doing very good work and had excellent mechanics. They turned out and put on the road some very superior cars. We are able to get our work done there just as cheaply as at Moncton, if not more cheaply. With some little additional machinery, these works will be in the first-class condition. We employ many of the island people, and I see no reason why we should not, if they are capable of giving proper service.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I wish to express my approval of this item. You will get as good value in Charlottetown as at any other place in Canada. We have skilled artisans there who turn out as good cars as can be found any where.
Have there not been very superior cars turned out there this past year ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, I was surprised that such cars could be turned out.

On March 1, I placed the following motion on the notice paper :
Copies of all orders in council, correspondence, evidence, finding of coroners, jury reports, papers and documents of every kind whatsoever in relation to the deaths of Bridget and Margaret Graham, wife and daughter of Bartholomew Graham, of Norton, King's county, N.B., who were killed at the Intercolonial Railway crossing at Norton station on the 3rd day of June, A.D. 1900.
This motion was unfortunately not reached, and I would like to ask the hon. minister Mr. HAGGART.
if he will bring down the information required V

Certainly.
Murray Bay harbour branch and Hillsboro' bridge, P.E.I., $450,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The estimated cost of the substructure is $375,000. The cost altogether will be $450,000. Eleven and a half miles of road are under construction, and thirty-two miles have yet to he constructed. The eleven and a half miles have cost close to $43,000, and we estimate that the total cost will be $170,000. Adding that to the estimated cost of the $450,000, will give $660,000. The $450,000 Is what will suffice for the coming year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What proportion Is paid by the Island government, and does the government of the Dominion provide driveways on either side of the railway ?

There will be an ample driveway. Under the arrangement with the Prince Edward Island government, they pay us an annual allowance of $10,000. We furnish sufficient accommodation for foot aud vehicular traffic.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Are tlie approaches maintained by the island government ?
All that they undertake to do is to furnish the planking upon the roadway of the bridge. The approaches are not being planked, but will be gravelled or macadamized.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It will be quite a long bridge, and have considerable traffic. AYho will pay the cost of lighting ?

My recollection is the island government provides for the lighting, and inasmuch as they are collecting tolls for the passenger and vehicular traffic, their toll collector will also look after the bridge and see that proper protection is afforded when trains are crossing.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understood the hon. minister to say that he was taking over the old bridge from the Miramichi river.

We are taking over the spans of the Miramichi bridge and putting them across this river on the superstructure. The hon. gentleman speaks of it as an old bridge, hut it is not at all an inferior bridge, but just as well fitted for the purpose and just as good as if it just came out of the shop. The bridge will he entirely satisfactory to everybody.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
This bridge taken from the Miramichi river Is twenty-five or thirty

years old, and was not sufficient for the service there. It was known to be antiquated and out of date.
Not out of date.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It was of no further service in New Brunswick.

The hon. gentleman must not ignore the fact that the Miramichi bridge is a good bridge. I could hardly set a limit to the life of such a bridge, but I believe that it would be perfectly good long after the hon. gentleman and his grandchildren have passed away, if we only have to use it for the same weight of trains and traffic as we have to-day. But I suppose that the hon. gentleman is arguing on the assumption that the traffic on the Prince Edward Island Railway will not at any period in the future need much heavier trains than we are now operating on the road. There is no question of inferiority in the bridge.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This bridge was built for a single track. But in Prince Edward Island, besides the railway track, you need a driveway on either side for carriages. How are you going to make this old bridge -perhaps I may be pardoned for speaking of it as an old bridge
Do not speak of it in a contemptuous way.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Well, I will not-but bow are you going to provide room for this driveway ? Are you going to roll out the iron again to make it wider, or are you going to patch it up ?

Surely the hon. gentleman does not imagine that there will be any difficulty in making the bridge wider. It will only be necessary to have longer cross beams and support. The span, the truss-all that portion of the structure is equally good, and will remain intact. The hon. gentleman did not catch what I said the other night- that there will be two methods, by either of which accommodation for foot-passengers and vehicles could be provided. One is by throwing out iron supports on either side so as to provide on one side a way for teams going in one direction and on the other side a way for teams going in the other direction ; the other is to widen the span and have the track so laid that you could have a carriage track on either side, or lay the track so as to have the driveway on one side. I do not see any difficulty about it, but I cannot say what method has been determined upon. A year or so ago we had various plans prepared, and the subject was gone over with the gentlemen representing the Prince Edward Island government. They criticised everything very
closely-I will say that for them-they were a little difficult to please ; but we succeeded ultimately, I think, in satisfying all their expectations and demands.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I suppose that is all right. I would like to know, in this connection, whether there will be any division or fence between the driveway and the rails ?

I think not.
Some resolutions reported.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understand that our friends of the opposition have a sitting of their own to-night, and that if we should sit here we should miss their criticism. Therefore, I move that the House adjourn.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: We on this side of the House desire to extend to the right hon. gentleman (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and his followers our thanks. We hardly thought that we were justified in asking for an adjournment of the House, but, as the right hon. gentleman has been considerate enough to offer it, we can only say that we are very much obliged for the courtesy.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 6 p.m.
Thursday, May 2, 1901.
